entry.evidence: The time scale of the iron solidification process and the associated convection (geodynamo) remain unclear.

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML with section and paragraph locators (jats_text)

steps.action: Poses the open question of the time scale of inner-core crystallization and outer-core convection, and whether locally concentrated light elements could change seismic wavespeed detectably.
steps.quote: The time scale of the iron solidification process and the associated convection (geodynamo) remain unclear.

steps.action: Sets up rivals for any SKS travel-time difference between paired earthquakes: a temporal change in outer-core properties versus differences in hypocenter location or focal mechanism.
steps.quote: they do not occur at the exact same hypocenters, and their focal mechanisms may be similar but different

steps.action: Designs a double-differential test: measure SKS arrivals relative to reference phases (Pdiff, Sdiff, PP, SS), whose sensitivities to a core change and to hypocenter changes differ.
steps.quote: it will affect the relative arrival times between the SKS waves and their reference waves differently from a change in earthquake hypocenters

steps.action: Finds the conditions in the USGS PDE catalog: M>6 earthquake pairs, 1990-2019, in different decades with epicenters within 100 km. The 21 pairs are reduced by depth, quality and source-radiation screening to 7 pairs and 55 SKS measurements at FDSN stations 98-145 degrees away.
steps.quote: We search for pairs of earthquakes that occurred in different decades and their epicenter locations are less than 100 km away from [...] .

steps.action: Measures relative arrival times by cross-correlation. At station COLA (Kermadec pair, 1997 and 2018) the 2018 SKS arrives about 1 s early when any reference phase is aligned.
steps.quote: the SKS wave from the second earthquake arrives about 1 s earlier than the SKS wave from the first earthquake

steps.action: Computes what the mislocation rival predicts for COLA. A 0.3 degree distance shift would give a 0.14 s SKS delay relative to Pdiff and a 1.9 s PP-SS differential. A 10 km depth error would give 0.1 s in SKS-Sdiff.
steps.quote: a distance change of 0.3° will also predict a large (1.9 s) differential arrival time between PP and SS waves

steps.action: Compares the observed differentials (1.1 s SKS-Pdiff, 0.15 s PP-SS, 1.05 s SKS-Sdiff) with the mislocation predictions and finds mismatches of up to an order of magnitude.
steps.quote: The observed δtSKS − δtSdiff differential time is 1.05 s, an order of magnitude larger.

steps.action: Excludes hypocenter differences and focal-mechanism differences (Fig. S2) as explanations of the COLA SKS advance.
steps.quote: [...] not be explained by differences in earthquake hypocenter locations.

steps.action: Generalizes the rival's predictions with a 1 km grid search over alternative hypocenters within 50 km of the PDE locations, computing SKS-minus-reference differentials for each (example in Fig. S8).
steps.quote: we perform a grid search on earthquake hypocenter locations at a 1 km interval in a spherical region with a radius of 50 km

steps.action: Checks the premise that mantle heterogeneity is negligible by computing synthetics in the 3D model S40RTS (SKS-minus-reference below 0.3 s, SKS-Sdiff about zero). The 0.5 s maximum uncertainty threshold is set from this result.
steps.quote: differential travel time measurements made on synthetic seismograms show that δtSKS − δtX are all less than 0.3 s

steps.action: Compares observed and grid-search differentials within ±0.5 s. Most measurement sets can be explained by mislocation. Five sets (0.8-1.1 s) cannot, and in these SKS arrives early relative to all reference phases (Table S2).
steps.quote: most travel time measurement sets may be explained by potential mislocations of the earthquakes to within the maximum measurement uncertainty of 0.5 s

steps.action: Extends the hypocenter search radius (up to 200 km) and finds the five anomalous sets remain unexplained.
steps.quote: increasing the hypocenter search radius does not change the result

steps.action: Excludes mislocation for the five anomalous sets and infers that outer-core P-wavespeed along those paths increased by the time of the second earthquake.
steps.quote: five anomalous measurement sets that could not be explained by possible earthquake mislocations

steps.action: Checks the epicentral-distance premise for pair P16: PP-Pdiff differentials below 0.4 s (Fig. 3) imply epicentral distances differ by less than 15 km.
steps.quote: Their PP and Pdiff seismograms show that their relative arrivals are small with δtPP − δtPdiff less than 0.4 s

steps.action: Establishes the pattern of the anomaly. Four sets come from pair P16 (1997/2018) and one from a second pair at CCM (1998/2015). All turn in the low-latitude Pacific in the upper half of the outer core. Only a few stations see it, indicating localized regions (Figs. 2 and 4).
steps.quote: The five anomalous SKS waves all turn in the low latitude Pacific Ocean.

steps.action: States rival anomaly geometries that give the same SKS advance: a small strong anomaly versus a large weak anomaly. Their waveforms should differ through diffraction.
steps.quote: In theory, a small-and-strong anomaly and a large-and-weak anomaly along the SKS ray path may produce the same amount of SKS advance time.

steps.action: Computes adjoint finite-frequency travel-time and amplitude kernels at ULN (Fresnel zone about 800 km at 30 s). Computes SPECFEM synthetics for a 6 degree, 4% anomaly and a 12 degree, 1.5% anomaly in PREM.
steps.quote: We calculate synthetic seismograms using the Spectral Element Method9 for different sizes of anomalies in the outer core

steps.action: Compares synthetic with observed ULN waveforms. The small anomaly produces defocusing and broadening that are not seen; the large anomaly matches much better (Fig. 6).
steps.quote: The same diffraction effects are not observed on the recorded seismograms.

steps.action: Rejects the small strong anomaly: the anomalous region cannot be much smaller than the Fresnel zone.
steps.quote: the size of the anomaly may not be much smaller than the size of the Fresnel zone

steps.action: Varies anomaly size (300-1200 km) and strength (1-4%) in SEM synthetics to fit the travel times and waveforms. Estimates a 1-1.5% P-wavespeed increase over a region about 800 km in radius and about 800 km deep in the upper outer core, with a stated size-strength trade-off.
steps.quote: a P-wavespeed increase of 1–1.5% in a region with a lateral radius of about 12∘ (~800 km)

steps.action: Checks that mantle ray-path differences are negligible. Ray separation at the CMB is about 0.1 degree (Fig. S4). SPECFEM tests with an anomaly on and off the ray path show a 1.0 degree shift changes SKS time by less than 0.1 s, consistent with S40RTS simulations.
steps.quote: SKS travel time differences due to ray path sampling different regions of the mantle are negligible for this dataset

steps.action: Opens the mechanism question, setting a thermal cause against a compositional (light-element) cause of the wavespeed increase.
steps.quote: The exact mechanisms responsible for the 1–1.5% increase in P-wavespeed in localized regions in the outer core over a period of two decades is unclear.

steps.action: Rules out a dominantly thermal cause. Sound speed in liquid iron at core pressure is nearly temperature-independent, and a cited dlnV/dT of about 1e-5/K implies a temperature drop of about 1000 K.
steps.quote: it would require an unreasonably large temperature drop (in the order of 1000 K) in a small region

steps.action: Converts the velocity increase into a 2-3% density deficit (for example 1-2 wt% more sulfur), using a bulk modulus insensitive to light elements. Estimates an order-of-magnitude flow speed of 40 km/year from about 800 km over 20 years, possibly faster.
steps.quote: the 1–1.5% of velocity increase can be more readily explained as a 2–3% of density deficit due to the high concentration of light elements

steps.action: Compares the inferred flow speed with flow speeds in published self-consistent geodynamo simulations and finds broad agreement.
steps.quote: which largely agrees with flow speeds in self-consistent geodynamo simulations16,17

steps.action: Refines the interpretation against Stevenson's density limits and global heterogeneity reports. The 1-1.5% perturbation is absent in most measurements, so it is read as a transient process, possibly compositional plumes and blobs from the inner-core boundary layer.
steps.quote: This likely indicates a transient process in the outer core at a decade time scale or shorter

steps.action: Lists further rival mechanisms left for future work: regional thermal convection controlled by lowermost-mantle heterogeneity, descending flows with suspended solids, and a stratified layer at the top of the core.
steps.quote: other possibilities should also be explored in future studies

steps.action: Tentatively disfavours a thin stratified-layer source: it would need 3-15% perturbations, which are least expected to change rapidly in a stable layer. The link to stratification is left open.
steps.quote: it would require large P-wavespeed perturbations (3–15%) even for anomalies with lateral sizes exceeding the size of the Fresnel zone

steps.action: Keeps the claim that the outer core is not well mixed on a decade time scale and that its heterogeneities produce detectable wavespeed changes, opening seismic monitoring of the core.
steps.quote: observations in this study show that the outer core is far from well mixed in a decade time scale

end.claim: SKS waves turning in the upper outer core under the low-latitude Pacific travelled about 1 s faster at the second earthquake, about 20 years after the first, implying a localized 1-1.5% P-wavespeed increase over a region about 800 km in radius that hypocenter mislocation cannot explain.

decisive_move.sentence: The hypocenter grid search with the 0.5 s criterion is decisive: without the five measurement sets that mislocation cannot explain, no temporal change would be claimed.

gates.evidence: Action: the question of a temporal outer-core change, and the mislocation rival, directed the choice of earthquake pairs and the reference-phase design (§1 ¶2), but the data are archival catalogue and FDSN records. Claim: the anomalous sets could have been explained by mislocation in the grid search, and the small-anomaly geometry could have matched the waveforms (§2.1 ¶2, §2.2 ¶2). Registration: the 0.5 s threshold is derived from S40RTS synthetics, but nothing is stated as fixed before the data were seen (§4.3 ¶1).

imports.item: cross-correlation measurement of relative arrival times
adjoint method for finite-frequency sensitivity kernels
Fresnel zone and wave diffraction concepts
equation of state and temperature derivative of sound speed in liquid iron

novelty_claims.quote: [...] observation was five anomalous SKS waves that travel faster through the outer core at the time when the second earthquake occurred
This opens the possibility of monitoring temporal changes in the outer core using seismic data.

limits: Only the published paper was supplied. The peer review file is mentioned (§A1.1 ¶1) but not provided, so no review sequence was coded. Supplementary Tables S1-S2 and Figures S1-S8 were not supplied, so the grid-search details and the measurement listings could not be inspected. Sub-claim statuses: the exclusion of mislocation for five measurement sets is closest to confirmed against the stated rival. The light-element (compositional) interpretation, 2-3% density deficit, is a best_explanation: the thermal cause is argued away, but other rivals (regional thermal convection, suspended solids, stratified layer) are explicitly left open (§3 ¶4). The 40 km/year flow speed is an order-of-magnitude estimate that rests on an unknown timing within the 20-year interval. The transience claim is an interpretation (§3 ¶3). The anomaly rests on 5 of 55 measurements, four from a single earthquake pair, with no formal significance test; the 1.5 standard deviation line is shown for reference only. The 0.5 s threshold appears to have been chosen in light of the synthetics; whether it was fixed before inspecting the data is not stated (inference). Whether the paper names a well-mixed-core position as a community view, and which work holds it, is not specified. The paper contains no explicit 'first' statement; the novelty claims listed are implicit.

disagreements.target: Stevenson (1987) limits on lateral density and velocity variations in the outer core
disagreements.support: The observed 1-1.5% perturbation far exceeds the theoretical limits; the paper reconciles this by noting it is absent in most measurements and is therefore transient.
disagreements.quote: We point out that the temporal perturbation of 1–1.5% in wavespeed observed in this study is not a general feature of the dataset

disagreements.target: The view that the liquid outer core is well mixed on short time scales
disagreements.support: Localized decade-scale wavespeed changes detected on SKS paths imply heterogeneities strong enough to be seen seismically.
disagreements.quote: observations in this study show that the outer core is far from well mixed in a decade time scale
